nameStory: The word 'exigua' comes from Latin meaning 'small' or 'scanty,' which perfectly describes this tiny jumping spider that's easily overlooked despite its active hunting lifestyle. Like other members of the Pelegrina genus, it's named after the Roman goddess of boundaries and limits, perhaps reflecting how these small spiders define their own tiny territories.
description: Pelegrina exigua is a diminutive jumping spider that embodies all the classic traits of its family in a compact package. These tiny hunters are known for their characteristic forward-facing eyes and ability to leap many times their body length to catch prey. Despite being small even by jumping spider standards, they're active daytime predators with the same bold personality as their larger relatives. You'll need to look closely to spot these miniature marvels as they patrol low vegetation and leaf litter.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small, even for a jumping spider - about the size of a pinhead or small ant, making it one of the tiniest jumpers you'll encounter

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Four large forward-facing eyes arranged in a square pattern, with the front pair noticeably larger and giving it an alert, almost curious expression

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact and stocky build typical of jumping spiders, with a rounded abdomen and relatively thick front legs that feel sturdy when gently handled

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in quick, jerky motions with frequent stops to assess surroundings, often turning to face you directly when approached

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Found close to the ground on low plants, fallen leaves, and debris where it can easily hide despite its active hunting style

habitat: Look for Pelegrina exigua in low vegetation, leaf litter, and ground-level debris in wooded areas and forest edges throughout New England. They prefer spots with some moisture retention where small prey insects are abundant, often found on fallen logs, low shrubs, and among dead leaves. These tiny spiders favor areas with dappled sunlight where they can hunt actively during the day while having quick access to hiding spots.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, beginning their hunting activities on sunny days. Look for them on emerging vegetation and warming leaf litter.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible hunting during daylight hours. Mating likely occurs during this time, though their small size makes observation challenging.
seasonality.fall: Adults may still be active on warm days, with egg-laying likely occurring before winter. Activity decreases as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Overwinter as eggs or juveniles in protected locations under bark, leaves, or other debris. Adults typically don't survive freezing temperatures.

funFact: Despite being smaller than many ants, Pelegrina exigua can leap more than 10 times its body length to catch prey - imagine a human jumping across a basketball court in a single bound!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with tiny wolf spiders or other minute hunting spiders, but the large, forward-facing eyes and jerky, stop-and-go movement pattern are dead giveaways that you're looking at a jumping spider. Remember: if it stops to stare back at you, it's probably a jumper!
contextualKnowledge: The genus name Pelegrina honors boundaries and limits, which is fitting since these tiny spiders are right at the lower size limit of what most people can easily observe without magnification. Their extremely small size means they're often overlooked in spider surveys, so actual distribution may be broader than records suggest.
compareHints: Pelegrina exigua is significantly smaller than its relatives like the Common white-cheeked jumping spider (P. proterva) and lacks the distinctive white facial markings of that species. Compared to the Peppered Jumping Spider (P. galathea), it's much plainer in coloration and smaller in size. Its tiny stature sets it apart from all other Pelegrina species in New England, making size the most reliable identification feature.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Pelegrina relatives in New England, the white-cheeked jumping spider is distinguished by those prominent pale cheek markings - the peppered jumping spider has more scattered light spots, while the yellowleg jumping spider has distinctly yellow-colored legs.

Among its Pelegrina relatives, the Peppered Jumping Spider is distinguished by its speckled 'peppered' pattern rather than the white facial markings of the White-cheeked Jumping Spider or the yellow coloration of the Yellowleg Jumping Spider.

Pelegrina flaviceps differs from its close relatives primarily in its yellowish head coloration - the Common white-cheeked jumping spider has distinctive white facial markings, while the Peppered Jumping Spider typically shows more mottled, salt-and-pepper patterning.
Among its Pelegrina relatives in New England, the Yellowleg is distinguished by its specific yellow leg coloration and strong preference for evergreen trees.
